newsitem.title: UK: UK shares in for volatile week, Wall St the key.
newsitem.headline: UK shares in for volatile week, Wall St the key.

text.p: It could be either feast or famine for the British share market next week as dealers and strategists believe the FTSE 100 could scale new heights before taking a tumble.
Although no one is absolutely sure what path the UK market will follow, market watchers are convinced Wall Street's will be the catalyst for either scenario.
"Fundamentally the UK market is in good shape. Earnings haven't been too bad and we don't have to worry about interest rates until after the election," the head of trading at a large brokerage said.
"But if Wall Street slides, the fundamentals won't do much but cushion the fall."
The FTSE 100 breached the 4,400 barrier this week, closing at record highs on four straight days, thanks to a strong performance on Wall Street and steady corporate earnings reports.

Investors on both sides of the Atlantic took a more relaxed view on the prospect for any near-term U.S. interest rate hike after Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan told the U.S. Congress that share prices may, after all, be fairly valued.

The bond and share market's initial reaction to stronger-than-expected U.S. unemployment figures for February was to take the view that the data would not prompt a near-term increase in the Fed's short-term rates.
But strategists warn that the market could be in for a nasty shock if the interest rate mood swings to a more bearish position.
"The first reaction to figures is usually the wrong one," said Richard Kersley, strategist at BZW. "On the surface, the U.S. numbers seem strong to us."
The U.S. non-farm payroll total increased by 339,000 in February against a consensus estimate of a 230,000 rise while the average work week jumped to 35 hours from 34.2 hours.
But average hourly earnings only rose by 0.2 percent versus expectations of a 0.2 percent increase, which calmed fears about rising inflation.
"The bias is still toward higher rates but until we see some signs of inflation, rates probably won't rise," said Kirit Shah, strategist at Sanwa International.
Shah expects the FTSE to trade in a narrow range of 4,300 to 4,500 over the next few months unless the Fed slips in a rate hike to counter any inflation threat.
U.S. producer price data for February, due on Friday, February 14 could spook bonds and equities if the figures are well above expectations, Shah said.
"Other than inflationary pressures, the only thing that will knock the market down is poor earnings," Shah said.

The head of sales and trading at a major investment bank believes the Dow Industrials, which has risen by more than 75 percent over the past two years, is due for a 200-point correction, which could begin next week.
"The yield on the long bond is stubbornly pushing back toward seven percent and U.S. second-liners (shares) aren't keeping pace with the Dow," the dealer said.
"A Dow correction will happen. I wouldn't rule out something happening next week."
Even if the Dow does take a dive, the FTSE may not necessarily slavishly follow it point-for-point lower, according to Corey Miller, strategist at Credit Lyonnais.
"The UK is in a better position to withstand the bad news of a U.S. rate hike," Miller said.
"We know UK rates aren't going up this side of the election and the market seems to have discounted a Labour victory."
"On our evaluations of interest cover and dividend cover, the UK market is still looking very attractive."

The market should show a slightly positive bias at the start of the week, possibly from short-covering and light, but selected bargain hunting, but this may evaporate as the week progresses, technical analysts said.
Technical analysts believe the FTSE 100 upside potential is limited next week.
"Market sentiment and momentum have adjusted fast enough this week to call into question the durability of any further rally," one analyst said.
"Judging by Friday's reaction to the U.S. payroll data, residual strength could soon slow down. I think it will be difficult for the FTSE to make much headway above 4,440-4,450."
If the FTSE fails to breach the upper barrier, the key index could slip to 4,340 by the end of the week, with some initial support at 4,390, he said.
Nine FTSE 100 constituents are due to report results next week.
The list includes Orange, Zeneca,, Rentokil, Schroders, Reed Elsevier, TI Group, Enterprise Oil, Legal & General, Reckitt & Colman, and United News & Media.
